WHO.title: Who decides for D.C.?
WHO.question: Seven decisions about life in the nation's capital. Who made each one: D.C.'s own government, Congress, or the president?

decisions.q: Whether a law the D.C. Council passes takes effect
decisions.detail: Every D.C. act goes to Congress for a review period (30 days, 60 for criminal law), and Congress can block it; it did in 2023 with D.C.'s criminal code rewrite.
The Home Rule Act lets Congress disapprove the city's laws, including its annual budget.

decisions.q: Who controlled D.C.'s police in August 2025
decisions.detail: The president declared a public-safety emergency and took control of the Metropolitan Police; the city went to court and the administration partly retreated.

decisions.q: Whether the National Guard patrols D.C.
decisions.detail: The D.C. Guard is the only Guard unit that reports to the president alone; by August 2026 the deployment had grown to 4,636 troops from 23 states.

decisions.q: Whether D.C.'s member of Congress can vote on final passage of a bill
decisions.detail: D.C.'s delegate votes in committee but not on final passage in the full House; whether she may vote on amendments depends on House rules set by the majority.
decisions.src: Washington Times, 2017; Office of Del. Norton

decisions.q: Paid family leave for D.C. workers
decisions.detail: D.C. Paid Family Leave is a local law: up to 12 weeks for a new baby, 10 for your own illness, at 90% of pay for lower-wage workers.

decisions.q: Clearing homeless encampments from federal parkland in D.C.
decisions.detail: In August 2025 the White House said U.S. Park Police had removed about 70 encampments, offering shelter or treatment.

WHO.notice: D.C. elects a mayor and council, but most of the big levers sit with people D.C. residents do not elect. Compare Denver, where most of the same decisions are made by people Denver voters elect.
WHO.yourCall: Is there a reason the capital should be governed differently from a state? Give the best case for it and the best case against it.

decisions.q: The lowest wage a Denver employer may pay
decisions.detail: Denver sets its own minimum wage, $19.29 an hour in 2026, after Colorado let cities do so in 2019.

decisions.q: Whether Denver workers get paid family and medical leave
decisions.detail: Colorado voters approved FAMLI in 2020; it pays up to 12 weeks. A separate 2020 state law gives paid sick leave at employers of every size.
decisions.src: Denver shared mirror (FAMLI; Healthy Families and Workplaces Act)

decisions.detail: An independent 12-member commission, created when voters passed Amendment Y in 2018, took the job from the legislature.

decisions.q: Whether Denver police use license-plate cameras
decisions.detail: The city council rejected a Flock contract extension unanimously in May 2025, the mayor extended it with new limits, and in 2026 the council approved 50 Axon cameras, 7 to 6.

decisions.q: How Coloradans vote, and whether people on parole may vote
decisions.detail: Colorado mails every registered voter a ballot, registers voters automatically, and since 2019 lets people on parole vote.
decisions.src: Colorado Secretary of State; Colorado Springs Gazette

decisions.q: Whether a low-wage Denver parent can get Medicaid
decisions.detail: Colorado expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act: adults qualify up to about 133% of the poverty level.
decisions.src: Denver shared mirror (Health First Colorado, HCPF)

decisions.q: Whether those Medicaid adults must report work hours from 2027
decisions.detail: The 2025 federal budget law adds work or community-engagement requirements for expansion adults from January 1, 2027, in every expansion state.
